strengths: Exploring discrete diffusion models (DDMs) over discrete neural audio representations (e.g., WavTokenizer) is an intuitive concept for mitigating spectral blurring and long-term degradation in audio inpainting.
The paper is structured logically from tokenization, diffusion training, to inference cross-fading.
weaknesses: Critical missing content and incomplete text: The Abstract ends with an unfinished sentence ('Audio examples of our proposed method can be found at'). Furthermore, both the Abstract and the Conclusion claim that the method was evaluated on the MTG dataset extending gap durations up to 500 ms, yet there are zero experiments, tables, or discussions regarding the MTG dataset or 500 ms gaps in the results section.

Lack of essential technical and algorithmic details: The paper does not specify how conditioning is mathematically enforced during the discrete diffusion reverse process (e.g., whether it uses masked diffusion replacement, posterior sampling, or specific classifier-free guidance). Key architectural specifications for the DiT model (layers, hidden dimension, attention heads, parameter count) and inference sampling parameters (sampling algorithm, number of reverse diffusion steps) are omitted, making reproduction impossible.

Superficial technical novelty: The proposed framework is essentially a direct concatenation of existing off-the-shelf components—WavTokenizer (Ji et al., 2024) and the DWDSE discrete diffusion objective (Lou et al., 2024)—without any domain-specific architectural innovations or novel formulation tailored to the audio inverse problem.

Insufficient evaluation: The quantitative evaluation is conducted on only 60 short music excerpts from MusicNet. There is no subjective listening test (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS), which is standard practice for generative audio inpainting. Furthermore, Figure 3 appears to simply overlay a single or sparse set of data points onto figures adapted from prior work without comprehensive comparative tables across all baselines.

Severe issues with writing, proofreading, and presentation: The paper exhibits multiple glaring typos, including in major headings ('Audio Inpanting using Discrete Diffusion Model' in both Title and Section 4), 'Continues Diffusion Models' / 'Continuousus', 'lustration' instead of 'illustration', and broken references (e.g., 'as seen in 6').

strengths: Exploring discrete diffusion models (DDMs) over discrete acoustic tokens (via WavTokenizer) is a sensible and interesting direction for audio inpainting, as it significantly compresses sequence lengths and potentially avoids continuous spectral blurring.
The paper provides a clear background discussion tracing the evolution of audio inpainting methods from classic signal processing to continuous and discrete deep generative models.
The method demonstrates encouraging objective results on the MusicNet benchmark across multiple gap lengths (50 ms to 300 ms) in terms of Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD).
weaknesses: Severe issues with manuscript completeness and polish: The title contains a blatant typo ('Inpanting'), the abstract terminates mid-sentence ('Audio examples of our proposed method can be found at'), and both the abstract and conclusion claim experiments on the MTG dataset extending gap lengths to 500 ms, yet neither MTG experiments nor 500 ms evaluations appear anywhere in the paper.

Limited technical novelty: The proposed AIDD framework is a straightforward pipeline combining an existing audio tokenizer (WavTokenizer) with an existing continuous-time discrete diffusion algorithm (DWDSE, Lou et al., 2024) and DiT architecture. The paper does not introduce domain-specific algorithmic innovations for discrete audio inpainting.

Lack of technical depth in method description: Crucial conditioning details during discrete reverse diffusion are largely glossed over. The paper does not formulate mathematically how the known context guides the generation of masked tokens during reverse sampling.

Insufficient evaluation: The quantitative validation is restricted to only 60 clips from MusicNet. No subjective evaluation (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS listening tests) is provided, which is essential for audio restoration and generation where perceptual quality cannot be fully captured by objective metrics alone.

Contradictory and unsubstantiated claims: The text states that 'AIDD out performs CQT-Diff+ across all metrics,' yet Figure 3 indicates that CQT-Diff+ achieves superior Objective Difference Grade (ODG, where higher is better) across several gap lengths.

strengths: Exploring discrete diffusion models (DDMs) over discrete acoustic tokens (via WavTokenizer) is an interesting and conceptually appealing direction for audio inpainting, potentially reducing sequence length and avoiding continuous time-frequency oversmoothing.
The paper is generally well-structured and provides a clear background discussion covering traditional inpainting, continuous diffusion, and discrete diffusion.
On long gaps (e.g., 300 ms), the model shows competitive or improved Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD) compared to CQT-Diff+ on the MusicNet benchmark.
weaknesses: Major discrepancies and phantom claims: The Abstract states, 'We further evaluated our approach on the MTG dataset, extending the gap duration to 500 ms,' and the Conclusion repeats that the model maintains performance on 500 ms gaps. However, the experimental sections (Sections 5 & 6) contain absolutely no results, tables, or discussions regarding the MTG dataset or 500 ms gaps.

Incomplete manuscript details: The abstract abruptly cuts off with an unpopulated URL ('Audio examples of our proposed method can be found at 
 1 Introduction'). There are also prominent typographical errors in the paper title and Section 4 heading ('Audio Inpanting').

Misleading claim regarding empirical results: The authors claim that 'our method AIDD out performs CQT-Diff+ across all metrics.' However, for Objective Difference Grade (ODG), where higher (closer to 0) is better, Table 1 and Figure 3 show that AIDD scores around -3.01 to -3.30, whereas CQT-Diff+ achieves significantly higher (better) scores around -1.0 to -2.0 for shorter gaps (50–150 ms).

Limited technical novelty: The proposed framework is essentially a direct combination of an off-the-shelf neural codec (WavTokenizer) and an existing discrete diffusion formulation (DWDSE / Lou et al., 2024) parameterized by a standard DiT. The paper introduces minimal methodological adaptations specific to the audio inpainting task.

Insufficient evaluation and missing subjective study: Audio restoration and generation papers typically require subjective human listening tests (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS), especially when neural codecs are involved (codecs can artificially degrade reference-based metrics like ODG and LSD while maintaining perceptual quality). Relying solely on 60 short clips from MusicNet evaluated with automated metrics is insufficient.

Lack of implementation and architectural details: Crucial details are omitted, including the size and configuration of the DiT (number of layers, attention heads, hidden dimensions, total parameter count), the reverse sampling algorithm, the number of diffusion inference steps, and how the known context tokens are clamped or guided during inference.

Absence of ablation studies: There are no ablations evaluating critical design choices, such as codebook size, tokenization models, number of reverse steps, contextual conditioning strategies, or the boundary crossfade window.

strengths: Formulating audio inpainting via discrete diffusion over discrete audio codec tokens (WavTokenizer) is well-motivated, addressing the challenges of modeling long-range temporal dependencies and phase reconstruction inherent to raw waveform or spectrogram diffusion.
The inclusion of span-based masking tailors the forward corruption process of discrete diffusion specifically to contiguous gap-filling tasks.
The proposed approach shows competitive objective performance (FAD, LSD, ODG) against prior methods such as CQT-Diff+ on MusicNet and GAN baselines on MAESTRO for gap lengths up to 750 ms.
The ablation study systematically analyzes the effects of span masking parameters and derivative regularization orders and weights.
weaknesses: Lack of mathematical clarity regarding the derivative loss: In Section 4.2, the loss compares ground-truth token embedding $e_i$ and predicted embedding $\hat{e}_i$. However, discrete diffusion models typically predict categorical transition scores/logits over the vocabulary rather than continuous vectors in embedding space. The paper does not specify how $\hat{e}_i$ is obtained (e.g., soft expected embedding via softmax, or embedding of the top-1 token) or how gradients flow through this operation.

Missing subjective evaluation and audio samples: Audio restoration and generation tasks strongly rely on perceptual validation via listening tests (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS). Furthermore, the abstract leaves the audio demonstration link completely blank ('Audio examples of our proposed method can be found at .'), preventing qualitative assessment.

Evaluation protocol and fairness concerns on MAESTRO: The authors note that they evaluated against prior literature results trained on the full MAESTRO dataset while AIDD was trained only on an unspecified 'random subset' ('Upon request, we will provide the full list'). Evaluating against external baseline numbers without strictly reproducible or standardized subsets raises comparability concerns.

Missing modern diffusion baselines on longer gaps: On the MAESTRO dataset (evaluating 375 ms and 750 ms gaps), the method is compared only against older GAN-based models (GACELA, bin2bin) rather than recent continuous diffusion models (such as MAID or adapted CQT-Diff), leaving open whether discrete diffusion is strictly superior to strong continuous diffusion formulations at these lengths.

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental, primarily combining established discrete diffusion formulations (Lou et al., 2024) with pre-trained audio tokenizers and standard span-masking techniques from NLP.

strengths: Formulating audio inpainting via discrete diffusion on discrete acoustic tokens (WavTokenizer) is a promising and conceptually sound approach, effectively circumventing the phase reconstruction issues of spectrogram methods and the high receptive-field requirements of raw waveform diffusion.
The proposed task-specific inductive biases—span-based masking and derivative-based temporal smoothness loss on embeddings—are well-motivated for continuous temporal signals like music.

The method demonstrates strong quantitative results on medium-to-long gaps (150–750 ms) on MusicNet and MAESTRO, outperforming prior continuous diffusion (CQT-Diff+) and GAN-based baselines across several objective metrics.

The model exhibits favorable training efficiency, achieving competitive or superior metrics with substantially fewer training steps and lower model complexity compared to continuous waveform/spectrogram diffusion models.
weaknesses: Lack of subjective perceptual evaluation: Audio restoration and generation papers typically require human listening tests (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS). Objective metrics like FAD, LSD, and ODG often have known discrepancies with human perception, particularly when evaluating audio generated via discrete neural codecs against continuous spectrogram/waveform models.

Missing audio demo link and samples: The abstract states 'Audio examples of our proposed method can be found at .', leaving the URL completely blank. Without listening examples or subjective tests, it is difficult to verify whether the reconstructions are perceptually convincing or suffer from discrete codec/boundary artifacts.

Missing mathematical precision in Section 4.2: The paper introduces $\hat{e}_i$ as the 'predicted embedding' in the derivative loss $\mathcal{L}_{deriv}$, but never defines how $\hat{e}_i$ is computed from the DiT outputs. Is it the pre-logit representation, an expectation over codebook embeddings $\sum_y p_\theta(y) e_y$, or a hard lookup? Because gradient backpropagation is necessary, this definition is critical for soundness and reproducibility.

Absence of a tokenizer upper-bound baseline: Discrete neural codecs introduce an intrinsic reconstruction upper bound. The authors should include copy-synthesis metrics (passing uncorrupted ground-truth audio through the WavTokenizer encoder-decoder) to isolate tokenizer artifacts from discrete diffusion errors.

Incomplete and inconsistent evaluation metrics across datasets: While MusicNet is evaluated on FAD, LSD, and ODG, the MAESTRO experiments only report ODG (PEA-Q). The rationale for omitting FAD and LSD on MAESTRO is unclear. Furthermore, the MAESTRO test set was downsampled to an arbitrary random subset, making exact benchmarking against prior work difficult to verify.

strengths: Formulating audio inpainting within a discrete token space via WavTokenizer and discrete diffusion is an appealing direction that avoids phase retrieval artifacts and reduces computational overhead compared to continuous raw-waveform or spectrogram diffusion models.

The empirical results on MusicNet show solid performance improvements over CQT-Diff+ on medium and long gaps (200–300 ms) in terms of FAD, LSD, and ODG, with substantially lower model parameters and training time.
The ablation study systematically analyzes the individual and combined impacts of the derivative-based smoothness loss and span-based masking.
weaknesses: Lack of subjective listening tests (e.g., MUSHRA or MOS). In generative audio restoration, objective metrics (FAD, LSD, ODG) frequently fail to capture subtle perceptual artifacts such as pitch drift, timbre inconsistency, or boundary discontinuities. Given that the demo link in the abstract is empty ('found at .'), perceptual quality cannot be verified.

The technical novelty is somewhat limited. Discrete diffusion (Lou et al., 2024) and span-based masking (analogous to SpanBERT / discrete span corruption) are established paradigms. Furthermore, the definition of the predicted embedding $\hat{e}_i$ in Section 4.2 is underspecified: it is unclear whether $\hat{e}_i$ denotes the expected embedding under the predicted token distribution, an argmax selection, or an intermediate representation from the DiT.

Evaluation on the MAESTRO dataset is limited: only the ODG (PEA-Q) metric is reported in Table 2 (omitting FAD and LSD), and the evaluation is conducted on a non-standard, unspecified random subset of the benchmark, which hinders direct comparability and reproducibility.

The investigated gap lengths remain relatively modest for a tokenized representation (300 ms on MusicNet and 750 ms on MAESTRO, corresponding to only ~20 to 55 tokens at typical token rates). Prior work such as GACELA evaluated gaps up to 1.5 seconds; demonstrating capability on multi-second gaps would significantly strengthen the motivation for latent discrete modeling.
